chunks: And Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn al-Aftas narrated, saying:

I entered upon al-Ma'mun; he drew me close and greeted me, then said: May Allah have mercy on al-Rida (peace be upon him); how knowledgeable he was. He informed me of something wondrous. I asked him one night when the people had already pledged allegiance to him, saying: May I be your ransom, I see it fitting for you to go to Iraq and for me to be your successor in Khorasan. He smiled and said: No, by my life! But before Khorasan, by degrees. We have a stay here, and I will not depart until death comes to me, and from there the Gathering [Place of Resurrection] without doubt. I said to him: May I be your ransom, and how do you know this? He said: My knowledge of my place is like my knowledge of your place. I said: And where is my place, may God rectify you? He said: The distance between me and you is great. I die in the East and you die in the West. I said: You are truthful. And Allah and His Messenger know best, and the Family of Muhammad. Then I exerted all my effort to entice him with the Caliphate and other ranks, but he did not entice me with himself.

key_terms.الرِّضَا: Al-Rida (the Pleased One), a title for Imam Ali ibn Musa
key_terms.الْعِرَاق: Iraq, the political center of the Abbasid Caliphate
key_terms.بَدَجَات: Degrees or stages, referring to levels of status or events
key_terms.خُرَاسَانَ: Khorasan, the region in eastern Iran where the Imam was held and died

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Rida predict about his death and the death of al-Ma'mun's envoy?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* highlights the Imam’s precise foreknowledge of his martyrdom in Khorasan and the Caliph’s death in the West, underscoring the concept of *‘Ilm al-Ghaib* (Knowledge of the Unseen) granted to the Imams. It illustrates the political reality of the Abbasid era, where the Imam’s refusal of the Caliphate was not a lack of ambition but a divine decree regarding his specific place of death and resurrection, reinforcing the Shia belief in the Imam’s spiritual supremacy over temporal power.
